title: Generative Analysis: How AI Enables Effective Leadership
text:
Despite the current economic struggles and a competitive job market, leaders are still being asked to do more with less—fewer staff members, for example—yet are expected to deliver results that keep up (or even surpass) their predecessors’ productivity. The challenge of doing more with less is an age-old dilemma and not one that will be solved easily or quickly.
That said, fortunately for today’s leaders, there is an abundance of new generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology which can help them increase their efficiency and effectiveness. AI-powered solutions such as content generators, automation tools, and chatbots are changing how we work while enabling leaders to do more with fewer resources. For example, content generation tools can help marketers create original, creative content for their website, blog, and social media in minutes. Meanwhile, automation solutions allow tasks to be completed quickly and accurately in the background with minimal effort, freeing time for more critical activities. And chatbots enable companies to quickly resolve customer queries and issues while reducing the need for human interaction.
With the right technology and tools, leaders can, in fact, gain a competitive advantage over their peers and drive long-term success for their companies. For example, consider OpenAI’s ChatGPT—a large language model (LLM) that can instantly generate human-like responses to almost any query. According to CNBC, “It’s the latest development in the world of generative AI, which has attracted billions of dollars in funding from tech investors.” This technology can help leaders quickly generate summaries from longer-form content, build reports and documents in minutes, and even find bugs in software code, all with a fraction of the effort and cost. Bloomberg recently went so far as to call ChatGPT “sophisticated” and even “magical.”
GPT-3, the LLM that underpins ChatGPT, is also being utilized by generative AI companies like Viable, a platform that can analyze large amounts of qualitative data like customer feedback to find the most urgent or essential themes. “Unstructured feedback is every company’s most valuable resource,” said Daniel Erickson, CEO of Viable, in an interview. He continued, “Although businesses have the technology to acquire massive amounts of data, there has been no way for them to effectively and proficiently assess it without much human capital. Until recently, analyzing customer feedback was manual, painstaking, and time-intensive—a daunting task requiring significant time and resources.”
Erickson added, “To revolutionize how leaders listen to, understand, and act on their customers’ needs, we developed Viable: an AI-powered platform designed to generate tangible insights through human-level data analysis.” Today, the company is helping businesses better understand their audience, make data-driven decisions faster, and save on operating costs with their generative AI solution.
Erickson believes feedback is a leader’s most powerful asset when used correctly and strategically. Because by proactively analyzing qualitative feedback from support tickets, social media, meeting transcripts, and more, companies can identify emerging trends like new feature requests or churn risks. This view is shared by Vijay Pereira, a professor at France’s NEOMA Business School. “With the power of generative AI, today’s leaders are equipped with the tools they need to make smarter, faster decisions than ever before,” Pereira said in an interview. “By leveraging generative AI to automate tedious but mission-critical tasks like data analysis, leaders can maximize efficiency and effectiveness while staying ahead of the curve in an ever-changing world.”
The Generative AI Market is expected to be worth $63 Billion by 2028, according to a recent report. The key, therefore, is for today’s leaders to harness the power of AI by incorporating it into their everyday operations. From automating mundane tasks to analyzing customer behaviours and trends, AI like GPT-3 can be used to help leaders make better decisions, save time and money, and ultimately drive long-term success for their companies. Here are three ways leaders can leverage generative AI:
1. Utilize automation tools to streamline processes and reduce manual labor
Automation solutions can help leaders save time and money by reducing manual labor. For instance, many everyday, tedious tasks such as data entry and report generation can be automated, allowing teams to focus on more high-value work.
2. Analyze data using AI-driven platforms to gain real-time insights into customer behaviors, market trends and product optimization opportunities
With the right generative AI platform, leaders can gain valuable insights into customer behaviors and market trends in real-time. Tools like Viable are revolutionizing sentiment analysis to help leaders make better decisions using customer feedback and optimize their products and services for maximum success.
3. Utilize chatbots to simplify customer service inquiries
Chatbots have seen significant improvement from single-purpose programs that generate automated responses to sophisticated, interactive, and personalized digital assistants. They are an excellent way to streamline customer service inquiries while providing a personal touch. New chatbots are contextually aware and leverage NLP to learn as they go, applying predictive intelligence to personalize responses based on user profiles and past behavior. Digital assistants can learn user preferences over time, provide recommendations, and anticipate needs. This can help create a more seamless customer experience while reducing costs associated with manual customer service inquiries.
These are just some ways that technology can help leaders make better decisions and drive success for their companies. However, while it’s essential to stay on top of the latest trends, it’s equally as important to remember that technology should be used strategically and with caution. As Erickson said, “AI should be used to augment human intelligence, not replace it.” The key to success lies in leveraging AI to help humans make better decisions faster while still understanding the implications of its use. With the right balance, leaders will find that they can achieve great success with the help of AI.
The power of generative AI is unlimited, and it’s up to leaders to embrace this potential. By leveraging the latest tools and innovations, they can maximize their efficiency while staying ahead in an ever-changing world. Erickson believes, “While most of the focus around AI in mainstream media currently centers around flashy tools like stable diffusion, the real value of AI will be in automating tedious but complex tasks that could previously only be completed by humans.” By implementing the right strategies, today’s leaders can use technology to their advantage and succeed in an increasingly competitive world.

title: Council Post: How Humans And AI Can Untap New Manufacturing Capacity
text:
Andreas Eschbach is the founder and CEO of eschbach, a software company that helps production teams work smarter and enhance collaboration.
Climate change, environmental concerns, the aftermath of the pandemic and global conflict are having an enormous impact on manufacturing. Meanwhile, fuel, food, microchips, chemicals and an array of everyday commodities are in short supply and experiencing inflated pricing.
Despite these challenges, manufacturers continue to innovate to become ever more productive while they work toward achieving a lower-carbon circular economy. What can manufacturers do to help solve these complex challenges as consumers place greater demands on producing more sustainable products while shareholders want better returns?
Many have turned to software and technology for productivity gains, such as using AI to unlock the value within “the hidden plant,” a manufacturing plant’s unrevealed and untapped capacity. By unlocking these insights, they may be able to make more informed decisions, increase operational and cost efficiencies and grow sustainability. In order to achieve these goals, however, they will also have to think deeply about the role of humans.
Valuable Tacit Knowledge
The tacit knowledge or "people experience" within factories, combined with the power of AI, can fuel innovations that will help humans solve complex problems and expand ingenuity in the process. AI-enabled systems, for example, can keep track of operational teams’ activity, positively impacting asset performance. AI can also help quickly retrieve collected data enterprise-wide and give instant access to relevant information to address any productivity concerns.
Expect to see greater adoption of innovative AI-enabled enterprise platforms to deliver better equipped operational teams, easier predictions of potential disruptions to the supply chain, faster troubleshooting production bottlenecks, such as spotting and fixing process inefficiencies. AI-enabled systems in manufacturing are picking up speed, as the market size is expected to reach $16.3 billion by 2027 from $2.3 billion in 2022, according to a Markets and Markets industry report.
The Complete System: AI And Humans
Enterprise systems’ new levels of AI capabilities have been compared to having multiple knowledgeable assistants at one’s side who continuously learn from operations, varied systems and multiple sites. They have all the data needed at their fingers tips and are readily available to answer difficult questions and deliver recommendations.
Since humans are not well equipped to process data and the complex patterns that appear within large datasets, it makes sense to use AI to easily sort through the sensor data of a manufacturing process and pick out outliers in the data. This information will clearly indicate which units may require the operating teams’ attention. AI can do this in a fraction of the time that a human would spend analyzing data.
To uncover those losses, it is important to contextualize the findings of AI with human observations. Complex problems require close collaboration of interdisciplinary teams to permanently resolve the root cause. The collaboration is especially relevant if manufacturing sites are operated 24/7 and people are working in shifts who can’t talk face to face.
In our volatile world, external circumstances have become the new norm and humans can adapt faster than AI. Humans are more beneficial to operations and productivity because they know the dynamics of the supply chain, as well as the company’s current needs and decisions. They can bring a business context that is not always successfully captured and/or visible in AI-enabled systems.
In fact, let’s face it: Humans can anticipate, imagine and judge changing situations, which means they can more easily shift from short-term to long-term concerns unlike AI. Such abilities are inherent in humans and do not require reprogramming, as would be the case with AI.
The Hidden Plant
To permanently operate an expensive production facility on high output, both humans and AI must work together symbiotically. If a corporation searches for losses in its entire global production network, this quickly results in the capacity equivalent to a complete greenfield plant—the so-called "hidden plant."
These are capacities that must be considered for the sustainable use of resources. When processes go wrong, people formulate workarounds on the fly. Over time, numerous workarounds become institutionalized. Therefore, processes, as they were designed, progressively deviate from what occurs in practice. What results is dramatically reduced productivity, profitability and sustainability.
With the hidden plant, small extemporaneous workarounds cause friction, which is already known by the operations crew. Very often, they have already found their way to some written form somewhere; for example, in shift logs, maintenance requests or reports of routine inspections. For the thousands of such records created each year, AI can help solve time-consuming investigations more efficiently. As part of the digital transformation, process engineers delving into potential problems use AI to uncover process similarities and patterns such as if the "product turned dark" or the "fluid showed black spots." Such pattern intricacies can be identified and provided to the decision-maker for determining how it will be handled.
Discovering an operating issue that is causing inefficiencies can be lucrative. Companies are often surprised by how much they can save after finding operational issues, such as insufficient coordinated transfer of intermediate products from an upstream process or long waiting times for results from a laboratory. Because those losses can be eliminated without investing one single dollar into hardware, they turn into a significant return on investment for a digital initiative.
With the right KPIs, such as OEE integrated into shift reporting, the data is in the hands of the operations crew, which empowers them with accurate data and makes them responsible to account for losses and increases their engagement.
However, unlocking hidden value using the right approach with both AI and humans can result in agile, lower-cost producers that can respond to disruptive market forces and deliver more value to consumers and investors.

title: Council Post: Beyond Innovation: Overcoming Challenges In Developing And Deploying AI Models
text:
Nir Kaldero is chief AI officer at NEORIS and Adjunct Executive for AI at CEMEX.
Artificial intelligence has become an important pillar for companies that truly want to reap rewards from their data-driven culture.
To date, data science teams have successfully figured out how to develop models and pilot them within a well-defined and limited scope. The problem, however, is that they are having a tough time figuring out how to effectively deploy and scale those models to capture exponential business rewards.
Pilots could be a wonderful way to prove value before heavily investing, but without deployment at the scale of those successful experiments being performed in the right way, the rewards and value may not be realized. I’ve seen companies hire data scientists and machine learning engineers to develop experiments with AI and achieve success. Still, when it comes to deployment at scale, companies struggle and only reach partial success.
The Challenges
There are several challenges in developing and deploying AI models, which can be broken into three main categories.
1. Misallocation Of Talent From Innovation Toward Support And Maintenance Of Deployment
AI is expensive to deploy. For every dollar spent on algorithm development, companies might spend around $100 on deployment, which is a huge chasm. Companies understand that if they have a successful AI project and they deploy it, they have to take a portion of their current teams’ efforts from building innovation to transforming the company, steering it towards deployment, support and maintenance.
Simply put, this is inefficient as talent is not allocated where it should be. The core data team has been trained and groomed as technical experts tackling business problems using data to transform the organization and find solutions. The business scales up based on the knowledge of its technical people. That’s what innovation is all about. However, developing a successful model and then working on deployment forces technical people to put aside business knowledge to focus on process excellence tasks rather than innovation, an inefficiency that must be addressed.
2. Lack Of Standardization
From AI development to the deployment end cycle, there is a lack of standardization, creating an enormous technical debt and costing time and money. Best practices would allow deployment processes to proceed at a faster pace. Moreover, this is more efficient from an economic perspective, reducing technical debt from AI development to the deployment end cycle. Lack of standardization is a roadblock, a disconnect harming proper deployment.
3. Change Management And Processes
It is crucial to realize the value behind AI. This is a business problem where technology chiefs must engage in strategic maneuvers so that the rest of the company understands the value of AI and steps toward deployment. Technical chiefs must ensure that people, culture and processes are adequately changed to accommodate the new technology implementation to realize the promised benefits.
The Solutions
1. Efficient Allocation Of Talent
The majority of those working on the AI team must always remain focused on innovation. They have worked hard at knowing and understanding the business and its problems so that they can transform the organization. Assigning the deployment, support and maintenance to the AI team will prove to be an inefficiency at scale.
Outsourcing is one solution, and there are two main ways to do so. One is by discussing tools that meet your company’s requirements. These might include cloud MLOps capabilities, DataRobots or Dataiku.
But this is only 50% of the equation. The other 50% is creating a talent muscle that is not necessarily needed to be included as part of the core AI team. Prioritizing tasks based on the projects’ funnel, searching for new hires or outsourcing tasks such as model monitoring, data pipeline and quality monitoring, versioning, and governance can reduce the burden created by diverting the core AI team time to process excellent tasks back into their main purpose of innovating.
2. Process Standardization
AI standardization is crucial from development to deployment. There is a need to create a standard methodology with a generic concept to fit many models that is also adjusted to the environment within a specific enterprise.
In other words, consider a general view tailored to work for every company, examining everything from technology to engineering and architecture. Creating one coherent standard methodology for developing machine learning models and deploying them can help companies solve issues like technical debt, speed-to-value, model deployment and cost ratio. This can rapidly shrink the development-to-deployment cost ratio.
For example, how fast can a team prototype a new idea? Can a team member move from one project to another and get oriented quickly? When it comes to deployment, is there consistency in the model’s development framework that can be put into production and maintained more easily?
3. Low-Level Vs. High-Level Tasks
The deployment phase of AI includes process-related tasks. Many are repetitive and can be automated, monitored or executed by talent separate from your team and outside your industry’s expertise. Manual tasks can eat up as much as 30% of the team’s time, so this is a low-hanging fruit for reducing costs while remaining focused on innovation. On the other hand, high-level tasks like research, development and experimentation are the ones the AI team needs to be focused on for innovation, and they require high business expertise.
Technology heads must also focus on change management, understanding organizations, people, business priorities and data constantly evolves. There are many moving parts within a company, and deploying an AI model requires strong influence over processes and people, including understanding how people consume information.
It is key to prioritize projects from day one to obtain commitment and sponsorship from the C-suite level to make sure those projects will always have a lucrative value. This way, no matter what changes happen within the business, those projects won’t have to be put aside as the added value will be understood.
Conclusion
Companies change rapidly, including C-suite executives, over the extended time it might take to properly deploy innovation. If the business is changing, then the technical environment is simultaneously changing, but the feasibility of developing and deploying the AI model must remain intact. That way, even as the organization evolves, AI always remains relevant and ahead of the game.

title: Edtech Enters Its Golden Age
text:
My son Leo was born to ride subways. His bountiful love of public transit has resulted in way more time than I ever imagined on trains and buses across the U.S. and around the world. Over Christmas, he badgered me to allow him to fly to Newark so he could spend the week riding New Jersey Transit in lieu of vacation with the rest of us. So when Leo began sending poetry about Toronto’s subway system (the TTC) to my parents and siblings in Toronto, it seemed as natural as a chime followed by “stand clear of the closing doors.”
Leo began with an ode to Line 4, which runs along Sheppard Avenue:
Line 4 Sheppard, oh how grand
A subway line that spans this land
From Don Mills to Downsview Park
It takes us where we need to start
Along the way, so much to see
Line 4 Sheppard, a path to our dreams
It went on and on from there.
This happened to be the same weekend ChatGPT was released, OpenAI’s third generation large language model (LLM). So my brother and sister correctly guessed Leo was playing with AI trained on an unfathomable amount of text data, including books, articles, and social media posts, and asked him to “write” poetry about other TTC lines. My sister requested the new light rail line being built along Eglinton Ave. (“The Eglinton Crosstown LRT, a glistening strand / Of steel and glass, stretching across the land”). My brother commented that the Sheppard poem was a fair depiction… of the Spadina Line, prompting:
The Spadina line, a serpentine beast
Winding its way through Toronto's concrete feast
…
So let us ride the Spadina line
And witness the city in all its shine
You get the idea. But you know who didn’t get the idea? My mother, copied on the bad subway poetry, was impressed as only a grandparent can be (“you have clearly inherited some major writing talent… It is delightful to have such multi-talented grandchildren”) yet baffled (“perhaps you should send a copy to the TTC head office”).
There are productive uses of GPT like fooling grandparents and dealing with bureaucracy; to satisfy the requirements of his student visa, one of our summer associates has already used GPT to produce a “2,500-word reflection on differences between the work culture of the U.S. and the country I come from” – an essay no human will ever read, let alone grade. But as GPT advises us to beware, there are highly unproductive uses, like cheating.
For the past month, cheating doomsayers have dominated the education discourse around GPT. For teachers who’ve toyed with the tool, panic is the order of the day: “What GPT can produce right now is better than the large majority of writing seen by your average teacher or professor.” On Tuesday, New York City schools blocked access to GPT, citing “negative impacts on student learning.” One Wharton professor demonstrated GPT could not only write an essay, but come up with the prompt, create a grading rubric, and grade its own answer (it received 80/100). How could writing assignments not be headed for the dustbin of history (or at least the history department)?
With the availability of GPT, every student is capable of producing passable paragraphs. So spring semester 2023 marks the start of a new era for education. Instructors will no longer be able to assign generic topics – “read the book and write about it” = malpractice. As if helping students become employable weren’t incentive enough, GPT adds urgency to project-based learning or learning-by-doing. And teachers will have to do more to help students make a connection between each assignment and specific critical thinking and communication skills they might wish to acquire someday.
But education’s immediate response will be to meet technology with technology – in our case, edtech. There are three ways schools will use edtech to maintain academic integrity:
1. Write in class
Use class time to ensure students complete assignments unAIssisted. To free up time and provide students with pathways beyond burger flipping, teachers will need to do some classroom flipping (i.e., have students watch pre-recorded lectures). Students perform better when teachers use technology to transform the classroom into the locus of assessment – not only summative writing, but frequent formative assessments administered in class via apps from providers like iClicker, Echo360, and CourseKey. Doing so allows teachers to ascertain whether students understand key concepts while encouraging peer learning, group problem solving, and project-based learning.
Unfortunately, many people flip out when you ask them to change how they do their job. In teaching, it’s not merely obstinance: flipping the classroom is as much work as developing a brand new course while delivery is more work than bulldozing through a course outline; teachers need to be on their game every class. And why bother when schools have no mechanisms to measure outcomes or reward change?
2. Write at home while we watch
During our year of remote learning, online proctoring became commonplace. Tools like Examity, Proctorio, and Meazure Learning lock screens and watch students while they write. But while online proctoring has become the norm for high-stakes tests, the cost of even AI-assisted proctoring puts it outside the bounds of regular assignments. More problematic, no one loves a panopticon, as seen in anti-proctoring petitions and protests. Some students claim online proctoring has harmed their mental health while others have successfully sued schools for invasion of privacy.
3. Cheat at your peril
Schools have been playing an extended game of whack-a-mole with technology-assisted cheating. When “model” term papers were first posted online – first in the hundreds, then in the hundreds of thousands – Turnitin was the first tech fix, detecting plagiarism by matching submitted papers against a database that absorbed all newly submitted work.
Can technology detect work created by AI? It’s not as though GPT doesn’t leave clues e.g., no typos, more likely to use common words (the, it, is). According to leading student writing company (and University Ventures portfolio company), Packback, the answer is yes. Right before the holiday, Packback announced that for spring semester, AI-content detection and flagging has been built into its discussion platform, Packback Questions, and will be released in the next few weeks for its new writing platform, Deep Dives. According to Packback co-founder and Chief Product Officer, Jessica Tenuta, “because large language models like GPT generate content based on the statistical probability of what word most likely follows the prior word in a sentence, this same approach can be used in reverse to detect the ‘signature’ of content generated by AI.” Packback flags text over a specific level of statistical expectedness and under a specific level of “entropy” (unexpected words and patterns). As of Christmas Day, early results suggest Packback will detect and flag the majority of all AI-generated content posted on the platform with a very low false positive rate (0.04%) – where students write like a boring machine. Packback continues to fine tune the technology.
Packback won’t be the only new edtech tool for catching AI content. Turnitin already has one product that can already detect some forms of AI-assisted writing and will be incorporating new AI-writing-detection capabilities across its portfolio later this year. Before long, schools will have a range of options and students will be required to submit even simple assignments through one of these platforms.
As schools allocate more class time to assessment, adopt online proctoring, and integrate AI-detection technology, GPT is bound to usher a lot more tech into the classroom. So the edtech-in-trouble narrative driven by last year’s decline in B2C edtech stock prices couldn’t be more wrong. Schools and colleges need help and 2023 is the first year it will be impossible to imagine education without education technology.
Thrilled at what GPT can produce – clearly they haven’t seen Leo’s subway poetry – some boosters are touting AI as “the biggest driver of productivity since the steam engine.” Imagine what GPT will do to improve customer service – it can’t make it much worse, right Southwest? But only if we get the education part right.
With edtech safeguards in place, the next step is for students to build the necessary skills to improve upon the new AI baseline. Taking advantage of GPT and successor technologies to produce superior work will require new technical skills like optimizing instructions for AI tools and changing parameters.
Just as the emergence of low-code/no-code platforms has eliminated coding as a prerequisite for tech jobs, GPT signals that leveraging AI won’t require a data science background, but rather an ability to utilize AI tools backed by a basic understanding of how LLMs work. It will be up to schools and colleges to ensure graduating students can use them effectively.
And so GPT should not only set off alarm bells for English teachers wedded to five-paragraph essays, but also for teachers of scientific and technical subjects. While our current approach is largely to teach the history of science – witness the physics grad who relayed to me her professor’s words upon graduation “congratulations, you’re now caught up to 1940” – more time is required on applying current and pending science and technology. Much of what is taught in STEM could be moved to history of science and profitably traded for applied technical learning. If we can do this, we’ll have all the ingredients for AI to become a useful tool for school work, but – thanks to edtech – not a shortcut (like Wikipedia).
Beyond tech skills, taking advantage of AI also demands new cognitive skills including selection, structuring, and determining when it’s wrong. As early adopters of GPT have already recognized, big data isn’t always right. In the 1948 presidential election, all available data projected Thomas Dewey would deny President Truman reelection. But young James Snyder (later known as Jimmy the Greek) had a hunch. Dewey had a mustache while Truman did not. So Greek surveyed Ohioans and found 4 out of 5 said they didn’t trust politicians with mustaches. He bet $10K on Truman at 17:1 and won. Jimmy the Greek’s first big score came from knowing when to go against the data. Students must be taught to look for mustaches.
As edtech enters its golden age, one thing is certain: when it comes to developing the new technical and cognitive skills students need to harness powerful AI, there will be new edtech tools to help.

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence Across Various Industries
text:
Key takeaways
- Potential applications of artificial intelligence continue to expand as more people adopt the technology
- AI usage is particularly prominent in finance, digital spaces (like social media, ecommerce, and e-marketing) and even healthcare
- For investors who want to put AI to work for them, Q.ai’s AI-backed Investment Kits could be just the thing
With the recent release of ChatGPT, AI-inspired modern art and the infusion of Elon Musk…everywhere, it’s no surprise that AI continues to dominate the discourse.
As the use cases for artificial intelligence grow, it’s inevitable that we’ll discover more ways it can improve our lives. And the space has plenty of oomph: The global AI software market is expected to reach $22.6 billion by 2025.
With AI’s popularity on the rise, we thought we’d explore a few especially promising applications of artificial intelligence.
What is AI?
AI, or artificial intelligence, is a complex topic with many layers. At its core, a “true” AI is a machine that can simulate human intelligence, behaviors and even emotions.
While no machine has reached that level, modern AIs can complete moderately complex tasks like:
- Solving problems and making decisions using data inputs
- Recognizing and interpreting visual information
- Recognizing, interpreting and responding to written and verbal language
In other words, artificial intelligence is software that’s programmed to “think” intelligently. Typically, AI models are trained using enormous amounts of information that help it “learn.” Advanced AIs can then process new data and draw unique, intelligent conclusions based on the presented information.
Modern applications of artificial intelligence
Artificial intelligence is a rapidly-growing field that has sprawled into dozens of industries. Companies and individuals use AI to perform repetitive tasks, analyze information and optimize other programs. From Google’s
Here are just some of the applications of artificial intelligence contributing to our technological advancement.
Chatbots
The release of ChatGPT gave the world a taste of what future chatbots could look like. ChatGPT interacts with users in a conversational way to answer questions and even challenge certain ideas.
But ChatGPT is an advanced, experimental iteration of a previous technology: AI chatbots. Thousands of companies have adopted AI-based chatbots to provide 24/7 customer support and resolve quick issues. As AI continues to evolve, it’s likely that chatbots’ language processing will grow more sophisticated.
Agriculture
Perhaps surprisingly, AI has also risen to prominence in agriculture. Computer vision and machine learning have produced apps that can identify soil deficiencies and provide planting recommendations.
AI also informs “precision agriculture,” whereby farmers use AI to:
- Analyze weather patterns to predict forecasts and planting schedules
- Determine the best crops to grow
- Address pest attacks
- Measure soil conductivity and pH
Plus, the combination of AI and robotics helps farmers harvest crops faster and more efficiently than human laborers.
Ecommerce
The ecommerce industry has capitalized on AI in a major way. Companies use AI to predict trends, analyze performance, assist with inventory management and more.
AI’s ability to track usage patterns and verify information has also made it a powerful tool in the fight against credit card fraud and fake online reviews.
Further, AI forms the basis of “recommendation engines” that show shoppers products based on their browsing history and preferences. And of course, virtual assistants and chatbots show up here, too.
Education
While education is still dominated by human personnel, artificial intelligence helps boost educators’ potential. Often, AI is used to facilitate automation in repetitive and data-heavy tasks, like:
- Grading homework
- Scheduling meetings
- Managing multiple online courses at once
- Sending personalized communications to students
- Creating or digitizing lectures and study guides
Yet again, chatbot-style AIs pop up – this time, to quickly answer routine questions and allow educators to spend more time on complex tasks.
Finance
The field of finance has leaned heavily into the use of AI at every level.
Customers can take advantage of AI to get information about their banking and investment accounts.
Banks and credit card firms rely on AI to detect changes in transaction patterns to catch fraud in action.
Lenders use artificial intelligence to predict and assess borrowers’ risk levels and make lending decisions.
Venture capital firms adopt AI to generate customized insights and financial risk management decisions.
And of course, robo-advisors and financial management services have leaned into AI to automate trading.
Healthcare
As artificial intelligence has grown more accurate, it’s made its debut in the medical field as well. On the less interesting side, AI helps administrators process data, schedule meetings, organize files and transcribe medical notes.
For more eye-popping illustrations of applications of artificial intelligence, consider how robots rely on AI to automate surgeries. Machine-led surgeries are more precise and less invasive, have a smaller margin for error and can run 24/7.
AI can assist in medical diagnoses by tracking health using wearable devices and indicating problems before patients are aware. Some programs have also adopted AI to help interpret body scans (like MRIs) to detect harmful growths with greater speed and accuracy.
Pharmaceutical companies even use AIs to analyze historical and modern data to discover new potential drugs.
Marketing
Another common application of artificial intelligence can be found in companies’ marketing teams. AI’s ability to quickly analyze data is useful for teams that need to quickly generate and act on insights. AI is used to:
- Generate campaign reports
- Improve customer engagement
- Personalize messages
- Deliver online retargeting campaigns
- Pivot advertising methodology mid-campaign based on new insights
Chatbots also fall into this category, as language processing plays a key role in analyzing and producing marketing campaigns.
Editing programs like Grammarly also make the cut, as AI can analyze grammar, vocabulary and sentence construction to keep brands on-message.
Social media
Social media makes another excellent use case for artificial intelligence. Firms like Meta and Twitter use AI to analyze massive amounts of data and generate actionable insights. Many companies also use AI to cultivate their social media brand.
In particular, AI can:
- Track user behavior to inform marketing and advertisement tactics
- Monitor comments to suggest new posts and accounts to follow
- Determine what’s currently trending
- Help generate targeted content based on demographic and behavioral data
- Combat cyberbullying and harmful or illegal content
In-home applications of artificial intelligence

Aside from testing out ChatGPT, you can find artificial intelligence in the automated driving programs used by Tesla, Audi, Volvo and others.
And whether you knew it or not, your email account likely uses AI to filter out spam and illicit content.
Your smart devices also use AI for facial recognition programs that log into devices and authenticate transactions.
Domestic robots, such as automated vacuums and lawn mowers, may also rely on AI to avoid obstacles and learn the best season or time of day to work.
And of course, Siri, Amazon Alexa and Google Assistance, as well as a variety of advanced home security systems, rely on artificial intelligence.
